name: Ivan Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice with a contractor that builds connection lines for the power company, mostly out to new solar farms and big electric-vehicle charging hubs by the motorway. We're growing fast, so every month there's a new site. My day is digging in poles, framing, running the tensioner, and a lot of standing around waiting for inspections. I'm still learning, my crimps aren't perfect yet, but I'm keen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does technology come into your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everywhere, for me. I use an AI assistant on my phone every day: to read the site drawings, check load tables, write up my logbook, even plan meals for the week. The crew think I'm a bit of a nerd about it. I live with Noor, my girlfriend, she's a physiotherapist, and I've got about nine months saved plus some money in funds, so I'm in a good spot to take a risk if one comes along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was overhyped, but the tools I use still help. I'd post something like: AI didn't take my job, it just writes my logbook. People would laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing much changes. Solar and charging hubs keep coming, so the contractor keeps growing, and I'd make journeyman in three years. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for the boring bits and spend the saved time getting better at crimps and rigging. I'd keep investing every month. And I'd start a small side thing flying a drone for building surveys at weekends, because I already have the licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, actually, because my plans all still work and I'd have a little side thing growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the drone side thing, if work's steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like having two things going. If the contractor has a bad year, I'd still have something. And it's fun, honestly, I like the flying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest risk in this world, if not AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates and the solar subsidies. If the government cuts the subsidies, the solar farms slow down and so does our work. But there'd be other contractors.

think: Privately, **solar and charging hubs** keep the contractor growing.
He'd make **journeyman** in three years and be fine.
do: Use AI for **boring tasks** and spend time saved on crimps and rigging.
Start a weekend **drone survey** side business.

steps.text: Use the AI assistant for logbook and load tables
Invest part of every paycheque in funds
Fly drone building surveys at weekends for extra money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where people like me do well, the ones who use the tools already. I'd tell the crew to learn the stuff now, because it's going to be expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. The planners and estimators at our firm would shrink, but the crew stays. And someone on the crew needs to be the one who reads the AI-generated drawings and spots the mistakes. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the boss if I can help test any new planning software, in work time. I'd offer to teach the older guys the basics. And I'd put more into my drone business, maybe get a better drone with thermal imaging for inspecting solar panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It feels like the kind of change I've been getting ready for without meaning to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a thermal drone cost, and is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four thousand. It's a risk, but I could pay for it out of savings and still have seven months left. Solar farms need panel inspections, and that's work I could get on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our estimator, Gerry, he's sixty and does everything on paper. I'd try to help him, but honestly, he'd probably retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a huge shift and everyone needs a plan, fast. I'd be posting about which skills still matter and how to learn them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a mixed bag. AGI by 2028 makes the planning and drawings automatic, so the office side goes. Then robots around 2031 come for the actual line work, and I'd only be a fresh journeyman. I'd have three years to switch to running or fixing the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a robotics maintenance course straight away, evening classes, and pay for it myself if the firm won't. I'd put more savings into robotics and power companies, because they'd do well. I'd also try to get the contractor to buy a robot early and let me run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'd come through it, but it's fast, and I'd be racing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robots don't need anyone to run them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still have money in those funds, and Noor's job is pretty safe, physios work with their hands on people. I'd look at something else. I'm not too worried about being stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the robots or plan your exit. I'd say it more nicely, but that's what I'd mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good warning, better than most industries ever get. Use it to get ready, learn the machines, and stop pretending it won't happen. I'd post a list of the courses at the technical college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'm a journeyman by 2031 with time to add robot skills before 2034. I'd be in a strong position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship, take a robotics course next year, and keep investing. I'd grow the drone side business into something real, maybe hire a friend at weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like enough time to do it properly instead of in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hire a friend. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Tariq, he's between jobs. He's good with his hands and I'd teach him the drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably whether the drone work survives too. AI will analyse the photos, so maybe I'd just be the pilot. That's fine for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse not to prepare. I'd encourage people on the crew to retrain early, while they're still earning good money. Online I'd probably keep sharing course links, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2036 I'd be an experienced journeyman, maybe running a crew. The planning side of running a crew would go to AI first, so I'd want to stay close to the tools. Robots around 2039 would be something I'd plan for over years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, take the robotics course in a few years, keep investing. I might buy a flat with Noor next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, this is the easy one for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're good. We'd buy a flat, maybe have kids, and I'd keep an eye on robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that I'd get lazy. With ten years, it's easy to think it's far away, and then suddenly it's not.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd be stuck, but because it's so fast. What would help is the contractor paying for robot training, and the government making it easy to switch trades without losing pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about side businesses. A lot of people my age have two things going, and that changes how scared we are.

headlineQuote: A lot of people my age have two things going, and that changes how scared we are.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old apprentice** building lines to solar farms and charging hubs.
He uses **AI every day** and runs a weekend drone survey business.
He has **nine months saved**, money in funds, and a girlfriend who's a physiotherapist.
He's **calm** in most pictures and only uneasy in the fastest.
His plan is to become the one who **runs or fixes** the robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it's **so fast**, not because he'd be stuck.
whatWouldHelp: Contractor-paid **robot training** and government help to **switch trades** without losing pay.
